extracted.intended_audience: educated readers of moral/philosophical essays (general public interested in Montaigne)
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading / extraction of evaluative principles and moral guidance from Montaigne's Essays (chapters on Cato, emotions, and solitude). The page is a Renaissance personal essay offering normative claims about judgement, virtue, emotion, and solitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not judge others by yourself
rubrics_metrics.description: I am not guilty of the common error of judging another by myself. I easily believe that in another’s humour which is contrary to my own; and though I find myself engaged to one certain form, I do not oblige others to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider each person according to their own model; allow many ways of living. Examples include approving the continence of Feuillans and Capuchins despite not practicing it oneself. Avoid confining belief to what you can personally imitate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue must be done for itself alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue owns nothing to be hers, but what is done by herself and for herself alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions performed for profit, glory, fear, custom, or other external motives are not truly virtue in the agent. Use historical examples (e.g., Aristodemus at Plataea) to distinguish genuine virtue from actions motivated by reputation or self-interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray and interpret virtue favorably
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Tis the duty of good men to portray virtue as beautiful as they can, and there would be nothing wrong should our passion a little transport us in favour of so sacred a form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging or narrating virtuous acts, prefer generous, favourable interpretations rather than maligning or inventing base motives. The author contrasts this with contemporaries who obscure noble actions with plausible drifts and ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize poetry's transcendence of rules
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a certain low and moderate sort of poetry that a man may judge by certain rules of art; but the true, supreme, and divine poesy is above all rules and reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that the highest poetry is apprehended by sudden inspiration and can overpower judgment; critics and judges should allow for experiences beyond formal rules when assessing great poetry or art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotions are multiple and can co-occur
rubrics_metrics.description: The soul variously and imperceptibly darts out her passions... we see not only children often laugh and cry at the same thing, but none of us can boast of never feeling mixed passions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect emotions to be singular or consistent; a person can simultaneously feel conflicting passions (joy and sorrow). Use this when interpreting behaviour (e.g., conquerors mourning defeated foes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not equate outward expression with inner motive
rubrics_metrics.description: Though the greatest part of our actions are no other than visor and disguise... yet, in judging of these accidents, we are to consider how much our souls are oftentimes agitated with divers passions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious attributing hypocrisy or deceit solely from external signs (tears, smiles). Consider inner complexity and multiple motives; avoid simplistic readings of appearances.

rubrics_metrics.name: True solitude is inward self-possession
rubrics_metrics.description: The true solitude... may be enjoyed even in populous cities and the courts of kings, though more commodiously apart. A man must sequester and come again to himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solitude is not mere physical withdrawal but the interior ability to depend on oneself, dissolve external obligations, and keep a private reserve (a 'backshop') of contentment unaffected by loss or plunder. Examples: Stilpo, Antisthenes, Paulinus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare for adversity by rehearsing deprivation
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Tis enough for me, under fortune’s favour, to prepare myself for her disgrace, and, being at my ease, to represent to myself, as far as my imagination can stretch, the ill to come.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentally rehearse poverty, sickness, death, and other misfortunes (counterfeiting war in peace) so that when adversity comes it is not new or overwhelming. This is a practical discipline for securing equanimity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not make external goods the foundation of happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Wives, children, and goods must be had... but we are not so to set our hearts upon them that our happiness must have its dependence upon them; we must reserve a backshop, wholly our own and entirely free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value possessions and relationships but keep a part of your contentment self-contained. Choose treasures that cannot be plundered (internal goods) so that loss does not destroy happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retire from public life when you can no longer add to it
rubrics_metrics.description: Solitude seems to me to wear the best favour in such as have already employed their most active and flourishing age in the world’s service... ‘Tis time to wean ourselves from society when we can no longer add anything to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Withdraw when your capacity to contribute declines; use remaining life for yourself. Retirement is fitting for those who have served publicly and now seek repose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ill company; guard against contagion of vice
rubrics_metrics.description: A man must either imitate the vicious or hate them; merchants who go to sea are in the right when they are cautious that those who embark with them be neither dissolute blasphemers nor vicious; look upon such society as unfortunate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select companions carefully because habits and vices spread by association. Use cautionary examples (Bias’s remark in a storm) to limit harmful influence from others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice moderation in using wealth (avoid excessive asceticism)
rubrics_metrics.description: I do not think Arcesilaus the philosopher the less temperate and virtuous for knowing that he made use of gold and silver vessels, when the condition of his fortune allowed him so to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When circumstances permit, use comforts moderately rather than performing extreme self-denial. Prudence, not rigid austerity, is the recommended stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Govern yourself by reason and conscience; maintain self-respect
rubrics_metrics.description: Let him soothe and caress himself, and above all things be sure to govern himself with reverence to his reason and conscience to that degree as to be ashamed to make a false step in their presence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal governance should be guided by inner standards of reason and conscience; cultivate self-reverence and avoid actions that would shame your own moral sense.
